Adam Hardy, who documented the drawings cut into the rocks around the site, argues the temple was meant to carry a Bhumija tower, the Malwa form with rows of small spires on each face, and would have been the largest Hindu temple of its day. The SGPC page gives the completion as both 1601 and 1604. Drawn by eye: the height of the marble storey, the dome and the Deorhi, the water level, the buildings round the walk, and the form of the Akal Takht. Which way the tank’s longer side runs is not given; it is drawn east to west. Inside there is no image; the scripture rests under a canopy, drawn here as a plain stand. The carving is a repeating pattern standing in for the real sculpture. Trees and grass are kinds common to the region, placed by eye, not surveyed.

how_it_was_built.t: The tank was dug from 1570 and finished in 1577. The foundation stone of the shrine was laid in December 1588.
Maharaja Ranjit Singh’s rebuilding and ornament ran from 1802 to 1839. The upper outer walls, the kiosks and the central dome were gold-plated.
The doors were faced in silver in 1830 and 1832. The four chhatris on the Darshani Deorhi were built in 1845.

how_it_was_built.t: The shaft was cut from a single piece of stone and the capital from a single block, then set on top. The shaft appears whole here, not course by course.

how_the_art_sits_on_the_stone: Marble is fine-grained, so it can be cut thin. The work is kept inside: the outer walls are plain, and the ceilings, arches and pillars inside are worked in layers, with the dome rising in rings to a hanging lotus at its centre.
drawn_by_eye: Sourced: the court size, the 52 small shrines and the colonnade, the dome over 7 m across, the plain outer walls, the date and the facing. Drawn by eye: the heights, the halls, the pillars and arches. The great hall was added in 1149; the cells came in two phases. The setting: the temple stands high in the Arbuda hills of Mount Abu, a range of valleys and steep slopes about 1,250 to 1,700 m up, with Guru Shikhar (1,722 m) at the north-east end of the plateau. Here the hills, the peaks and the drop to the plains are of the right order of height, but every distance is squeezed so they fit in view; Guru Shikhar really lies more than ten kilometres away by road.
